name: Khaki Grey
lede: Khaki Grey is a moderate yellowish brown standardized not by a color dictionary but by RAL, the German industrial color system, in 1927, and one of the most common matches in our entire painting archive.

sections.title: An industrial standard, not a dictionary entry
sections.body:
RAL lists Khaki Grey as RAL 7008, and the hex value in our library is an approximate screen conversion of that standard [1]. No Ridgway, Maerz and Paul or ISCC-NBS entry repeats the name in our library [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[greyish-brown]], [[bronze]] and [[medal-bronze]], at 3.7, 
The closest common color word in our library is [[sepia|Sepia]], under ten units away in CIEDE2000 [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A color within six units of Khaki Grey covers at least five percent of the canvas in 4,828 of our 23,781 paintings, 20.3 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 2,774, one of the most common matches in the entire archive [2]. That ranks it ahead of 98 percent of the named colors we track [2]. It peaks in the 1700s, in 452 of 3,449 paintings, at 13.1 percent of that century's paintings, barely above the archive's overall rate, and it most often plays a light, in 31 percent of its 2,774 appearances [2].

Salomon van Ruysdael is its most devoted painter, in seven of his 13 paintings here, 3.4 times the rate of the museums those works come from [2]. It shares canvases with [[water-grey|Water Grey]] and [[indigo-tea|Indigo Tea]] more than chance would predict, with lifts of 2.7 and 2.0 [2]. In printed English the phrase itself peaked in the 1980s, more than fifty years after RAL standardized the swatch in 1927 [2]. The earliest matching painting dates to 900, by Zhao Guangfu, 1,027 years before that standard — a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof the color existed as a dye that early, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].
